## Benchmark datasets

### BixBench-Verified-50

BixBench evaluates agents on open-ended computational-biology analyses that require data inspection, analytical planning, tool use and interpretation of a final result \[BixBench ref\].
We used BixBench-Verified-50, a curated subset containing 50 questions from 33 BixBench data capsules.
The subset was developed to reduce benchmark-related errors while retaining open-ended analytical tasks.
Questions were reviewed with domain experts for correctness of the ground truth, sufficiency of the supplied context and clarity of the expected answer.
Seventeen of the 50 questions were revised relative to the original BixBench release.
Revisions included clarifying question wording, specifying tools or methods when required by the reference analysis and correcting expected answers where necessary.

Each benchmark item contains a question, an ideal answer, an associated data capsule and a predefined evaluation mode.
The data capsules contain the input data required for the analysis and the reference analysis notebook.
Agents received the benchmark question and task input data but were not provided with the reference notebook or ideal answer during evaluation.

We used the BixBench-Verified-50 task definitions and acceptance criteria as the basis for evaluation.
Benchmark-specific changes identified during our experiments were recorded explicitly rather than applied retrospectively without documentation.
These included changes associated with evolving external databases, software-version dependencies and reference values that could not be regenerated from the deposited input data.
Task-level acceptance criteria and benchmark modifications are reported in Supplementary Table 1.

### CompBioBench

CompBioBench v1 comprises 100 computational-biology tasks with objectively gradable answers.
The benchmark spans genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, single-cell analysis, human genetics and machine learning \[CompBioBench ref\].
Questions were designed to require multi-step reasoning, specialized tool use, bespoke code and, for some tasks, retrieval of external data or software.
Synthetic or augmented datasets and metadata-recovery tasks were used to provide unambiguous ground truths without prescribing the analytical route.

We evaluated all 100 CompBioBench v1 tasks.
Each item consists of a free-text question, associated input files when required and a predefined reference answer.
Agents received the original task question and corresponding input data but were not provided with the reference answer, benchmark solution, reference execution traces or selected examples from the original study.

The analytical strategy was not prescribed in either execution condition.
Agents could independently select the tools, intermediate analyses and external resources required to derive the answer.
This preserves a central feature of CompBioBench: tasks specify the required result but generally do not specify the computational path used to obtain it.

All results reported in this study were generated by the executions described below.
No value was taken from a published leaderboard, and no value was estimated, extrapolated or otherwise predicted from partial data.

## Input-data preparation and versioning

For BixBench-Verified-50, the input datasets used in the reported experiments were frozen before evaluation and archived on Zenodo (record 21115010) to preserve the exact data version used in this study.
This avoided dependence on subsequent changes to the upstream dataset or external resources.

For CompBioBench, task input files were obtained from the benchmark release used for this study \[release, commit or archive identifier\].
The same task inputs were used under both execution conditions

For Galaxy-API-code experiments in both benchmark suites, task inputs were preloaded into Galaxy seed histories.
Each run copied the corresponding seed history into a new analysis history before execution.
This avoided repeated data transfer while ensuring that independent runs began with identical input datasets.
Open-ended-code runs received the corresponding task inputs in their local execution workspace.
Seed histories were prepared for both BixBench-Verified-50 and CompBioBench.

## Models and agent harness

We evaluated four model configurations: GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Luna and DeepSeek V4 Pro.
Primary benchmark evaluations were executed through Codex version 26.826.
DeepSeek V4 Pro was accessed through \[provider endpoint and harness configuration used to serve a non-OpenAI model through Codex\].
GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol and DeepSeek V4 Pro were run at high reasoning effort.
GPT-5.6 Luna was run at maximum reasoning effort because \[reason\].
Reasoning effort was held constant across execution conditions for every model, so it does not contribute to the contrast between conditions.
Exact model identifiers, provider configurations, reasoning-effort settings and access dates are reported in Supplementary Table 3.

For each benchmark item, the agent received the question, access to the corresponding input data and instructions defining the execution condition.
Reference answers, reference analyses and subsequent error-analysis annotations were excluded from the agent context.

## Execution conditions

Each model was evaluated under two execution conditions: open-ended code and Galaxy-API code.
Within each benchmark, the question and input datasets were held fixed between conditions; only the execution substrate differed.

Under open-ended code, the agent could determine its own computational strategy and solve the task through direct programmatic execution.
The agent could write and execute code, use command-line programs, install or access required software and retrieve external resources when permitted by the task.
This condition provided the direct code-execution baseline.

Under Galaxy-API code, the agent was instructed to perform analytical computation through Galaxy and to interact with the platform programmatically.
Experiments used Galaxy version 26.1.2.dev0 (commit \[hash\]).
The agent could use code to interact with the Galaxy API, including creating or copying histories, identifying tools, configuring parameters, submitting jobs, monitoring execution and inspecting outputs.
The analytical route was not predefined.
Agents independently selected the Galaxy tools, parameters and sequence of operations required to answer each question.

Network and external-resource access was equivalent in the two conditions: \[state the access policy applied, and confirm that agents under Galaxy-API code could retrieve external data and reference resources on the same terms as under open-ended code\].
This is relevant because several CompBioBench tasks require comparison against external databases.

Galaxy tool versions available on the server were not modified to reproduce software environments associated with the original benchmark reference analyses.
Tool identity, version, parameters, input datasets and generated outputs were retained in the Galaxy history.
Software-version differences between Galaxy and the benchmark reference environment were therefore treated as properties of the managed execution environment rather than normalized away.

The complete system prompts and execution policies for both conditions are provided with the evaluation code.

## Experimental design

BixBench-Verified-50 and CompBioBench were analyzed as separate benchmark experiments.

For BixBench-Verified-50, each of the 50 questions was evaluated with four model configurations under two execution conditions and three independent replicates: 50 questions x 4 models x 2 conditions x 3 replicates = 1,200 runs.
Each execution condition contained 600 runs, and each model contributed 150 runs per condition.

For CompBioBench, each of the 100 questions was evaluated using the same four model configurations, two execution conditions and three independent replicates: 100 questions x 4 models x 2 conditions x 3 replicates = 2,400 runs.
Each execution condition contained 1,200 runs, and each model contributed 300 runs per condition.

Across the two benchmark suites, the experimental design comprised 3,600 agent runs.

Replicates represented independent agent trajectories.
Replicate numbers were used only to identify repeated runs and did not define matched observations between execution conditions.
For example, replicate 1 under Galaxy-API code was not initialized, seeded or otherwise experimentally matched to replicate 1 under open-ended code.
Replicate indices were therefore not treated as paired observations.

Each run began from a fresh agent trajectory and an independent local workspace or Galaxy history.
Runs that terminated without producing a scoreable final answer, including runs exceeding the predefined execution limit of \[time limit\], were scored as incorrect.
The number of such runs per benchmark, model and execution condition is reported in Supplementary Table 4.

## Answer evaluation

The primary outcome for both benchmarks was final-answer accuracy.
Each run produced one final response that was evaluated against the corresponding benchmark acceptance criterion.
Correctness was binary and no partial credit was assigned.
Scoring was performed automatically against predefined criteria without reference to the execution condition of the run.

### BixBench-Verified-50

Evaluation followed the verifier associated with each BixBench-Verified-50 item.
BixBench-Verified-50 comprises 17 string-verifier, 13 range-verifier and 20 LLM-verifier questions.
String-verifier tasks required agreement with the predefined accepted output, and range-verifier tasks accepted numerical values within the specified range.
LLM-verifier tasks were evaluated using the benchmark's semantic-answer verification procedure with \[verifier model, version and provider\] and the verification prompt provided with the evaluation code.
The verifier was applied identically to runs from both execution conditions and \[was / was not\] one of the four evaluated model configurations.

Where our audit identified a documented reason for more than one technically valid result, such as an external database update or architecture-dependent output, the scoring criterion was defined before comparison of execution conditions and applied identically to all models and runs.
Complete task-level scoring criteria and benchmark-specific changes are reported in Supplementary Table 1.

### CompBioBench

CompBioBench evaluation followed the task-specific answer requirements defined by the benchmark.
The benchmark uses binary evaluation against predefined answers and specifies the required output representation within each question.
Numerical tasks include the rounding or tolerance required for evaluation where applicable.
The same acceptance criterion was applied to Galaxy-API-code and open-ended-code runs.

For each benchmark, accuracy was calculated as the number of correct runs divided by the number of evaluated runs.
Aggregate BixBench-Verified-50 accuracy was calculated over 600 runs per execution condition, and model-specific accuracy over 150 runs per model and condition.
Aggregate CompBioBench accuracy was calculated over 1,200 runs per execution condition, and model-specific accuracy over 300 runs per model and condition.

## Analysis of execution trajectories

Agent execution traces were retained for both execution conditions to examine how agents approached individual tasks.

For BixBench-Verified-50, we performed a run-level audit of recurrent failures and questions showing differences between execution conditions.
All 22 questions with at least one incorrect run were included in the task-level failure analysis.
For each audited run, we examined the final answer, execution trace and generated analysis.
Galaxy histories were additionally inspected for Galaxy-API-code runs when available.

Root causes were assigned only when supported by execution evidence.
Failure mechanisms were grouped into analytical reasoning, analysis scope or task interpretation, output interpretation or post-processing, software-version dependency, benchmark data or reference provenance, and resource or execution failure.
Cases for which the available trace did not support a definitive explanation were classified as pending audit.
A task-level category represents the dominant audited mechanism and does not imply that every failed trajectory for that task failed for the same reason.
Failure counts and classifications are reported in Supplementary Table 2.

For CompBioBench, item-level success counts were compared between execution conditions and representative tasks with condition-specific outcomes were examined in detail.
We inspected the sequence of analytical operations, intermediate checks, external-resource use and final-answer derivation.
For Galaxy-API-code runs, the corresponding Galaxy history was used to reconstruct tool execution and intermediate datasets where available.
These analyses were descriptive and were used to characterize how changes in execution substrate altered the analytical trajectory rather than to redefine task correctness.
Statements in the Results describing analytical trajectories are therefore qualitative summaries of audited runs and were not subjected to statistical testing.

Condition-specific comparisons used success counts within each question and execution condition.
Independent replicate indices were not paired between conditions.

## Model-interaction analysis

Model interaction was quantified for the CompBioBench experiments using provider-reported token counts associated with each run.
Input and output tokens were recorded separately.
Total tokens were defined as input plus output tokens.
Reasoning tokens reported as part of model output were not added a second time.
Cached input tokens were included at full weight within total input tokens; because trajectory length differs between execution conditions, totals excluding cached input tokens are reported alongside the primary totals in Supplementary Table 4.

Provider usage records were available for 2,398 of 2,400 CompBioBench runs; one GPT-5.5 Galaxy-API run and one DeepSeek V4 Pro open-ended run lacked a usage record.
Missing token values were not imputed.

Token totals include every run with a usage record, irrespective of whether the run produced a correct or scoreable answer.
Runs terminating at the execution limit therefore contribute their full token cost.
The number and token share of such runs in each execution condition are reported in Supplementary Table 4 so that their contribution to the reported fold change can be assessed.

Total model interaction was calculated by summing reported tokens within each model and execution condition.
The fold change associated with Galaxy-API code was calculated as the Galaxy-API total divided by the corresponding open-ended-code total.
The same calculation was applied to the aggregate totals across all four models.

## Storage measurement

Token counts quantify interaction with the model and were analyzed separately from the computational resources used to execute scientific jobs.

Storage consumed by intermediate CompBioBench datasets was measured in both execution conditions: from the Galaxy history for Galaxy-API-code runs and from the local execution workspace for open-ended-code runs.
Measurements report \[peak / cumulative\] storage per run and \[include / exclude\] datasets deleted or purged during execution.
Input datasets copied from the seed history \[were / were not\] included in the reported totals, so that the two conditions are compared on the same basis.
The measurement procedure is described in \[procedure\], and per-task values are reported in Supplementary Table 5.

## Statistical analysis

BixBench-Verified-50 and CompBioBench were analyzed independently.
For each benchmark, the primary comparison was the difference in final-answer accuracy between Galaxy-API code and open-ended code.
Because each benchmark question contributed repeated observations across models and replicates, individual runs were not assumed to be statistically independent.

The association between execution condition and correctness was assessed using a generalized linear mixed-effects model with a binomial error distribution and logit link.
Run correctness was the binary dependent variable, execution condition was the primary fixed effect and model configuration was included as a fixed effect.
Benchmark question was included as a random intercept to account for repeated observations within questions.
A condition-by-model interaction term was included to assess whether the execution-condition effect differed between model configurations; per-model accuracy differences quoted in the Results are otherwise descriptive.

Open-ended code was used as the reference execution condition.
The execution-condition effect is reported as an odds ratio with a two-sided 95% confidence interval and P value.
Model configuration was treated as a fixed effect because the four models represented prespecified experimental configurations rather than a random sample from a population of models.

Uncertainty in the absolute accuracy difference was estimated independently using a question-clustered nonparametric bootstrap.
Benchmark questions were sampled with replacement while retaining all model, execution-condition and replicate observations belonging to each selected question.
Aggregate Galaxy-API-code and open-ended-code accuracy was recalculated for each bootstrap sample, and their difference was recorded.
The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of \[N\] bootstrap replicates defined the 95% confidence interval.

The mixed-effects model and bootstrap address the primary accuracy comparison.
Token totals and storage measurements are reported as descriptive summaries and were not subjected to hypothesis testing.

All statistical tests were two-sided.
Analyses were performed using \[software, version and packages\].
